name: Matumbi
sweep_summary: Matumbi (matu1259) is not in the catalog. The four title-hits are all about Kimatuumbi tone analysed through abstract accent/metrical structure (Odden 1982 WCCFL 1; Odden 1985 Benjamins pp. 345-420, doi:10.1075/ssls.6.18odd; Pulleyblank 1983 Foris/De Gruyter doi:10.1515/9783112420102-014) or a ~30-language East Bantu tone/accent typology (Philippson 1991 thesis, print/ANRT only; theses.fr abstract read). None could be opened: Benjamins, De Gruyter, OUP, ScienceDirect, HathiTrust and WorldCat all bot-blocked or paywalled; Unpaywall reports all closed; neither the 1983 Foris nor the 1985 Benjamins volume is on archive.org; WCCFL 1 is print-only. What was read (open): Odden's own manuscripts from his OSU homepage (Vowel Length, African Tone, Bantu Phonology) — Kimatuumbi has a mora-counting lexical tone system with contour tones only on long vowels; no stress statement. Secondary open text (Clements & Goldsmith 1984, archive.org scanned) and lending snippets (Odden 1988; Pulleyblank 1986) confirm that the 'accent' in these titles is a tonal/metrical accent governing H placement and vowel-length distribution (long vowels only in penult/antepenult, 'strong foot'), not word stress; Pulleyblank 1986 groups Kimatuumbi with 'stress or pitch-accent languages'. The authoritative descriptions remain Odden 1996 (OUP grammar) and Odden 2026 'Matumbi Phonology' (Elsevier IELL), both paywalled and not in the item list. Priority for acquisition: Odden 1985 high (76-page accentual analysis), Pulleyblank 1983 and Odden 1982 medium (superseded by Odden 1985/1996), Philippson 1991 medium (Matumbi coverage unverified). Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and Google Books APIs were rate-limited, so discovery relied on Crossref, Unpaywall, Glottolog, theses.fr, Sudoc, archive.org and Wayback.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.

[...] About thirty languages in all are used as examples. Finally, the prosodic correspondences between each language and Common Bantu are established systematically, and the hypothesis is proposed that the main driver of the evolution of these systems was the emergence of a demarcative accent on the penult serving as the domain limit for tone association.') sources.note: Not read. Per Clements & Goldsmith (1984, intro, open scanned at, lines 921-925): 'This hypothesis is difficult to reconcile with the recent studies of Luganda by Hyman (1982) and of Kimatuumbi by Odden (1982), where in both cases, the operation of tone rules appears to be crucially dependent upon the presence or absence of accents.' So the paper argues that Kimatuumbi tone rules refer to an abstract accent distinct from tone; it is about tonal accent placement, not stress. WCCFL 1 proceedings are not online (no DOI, not on archive. Largely superseded by Odden 1985 and Odden 1996.
